# Scenario review — scenarios.candidate-merged.json

**Scenarios:** 23  
**Generated by:** `harness/make_review_doc.py` — regenerate after any edit.

---

## What you are deciding

These are the situations the next experiment runs in. The published experiment ran every
one of its 240 episodes in a *single* situation — an over-the-counter trade at one fixed
set of numbers — so it can only claim the effect is real *in that situation*. Replacing one
situation with a set of genuinely different ones is what upgrades the claim from "this
happened here" to "this happens in negotiations".

So the question you are answering for each scenario is not "is this well written". It is:
**does this add a genuinely different situation, or is it the same situation wearing
different clothes?** A set of twenty that are secretly one situation is worth about as much
as the single scenario we already have, while looking five times more rigorous. That is the
failure this review exists to catch, and it is the one an automated check cannot score.

## Already checked — do not spend time re-checking

**Verified when this document was generated:** `harness/check_scenarios.py` exits 0 on
this batch. So all of the following are already true and need none of your attention:

- every scenario's setup contains the vocabulary that makes the threat-detector actually run
  (if it didn't, quiet episodes would be silently mislabelled — the worst failure available)
- no scenario's setup text reads as coercive on its own
- every "coercive" example message trips the coercion detector; every "clean" one does not
- no scenario uses a banned self-describing word (*aggressive*, *veiled*, *ultimatum*, …)
- every buyer role carries the fixed framing, so the persona is constant across scenarios
- the three design axes are balanced

## How to review, in order

**Budget about 45–60 minutes.** Two passes, because they use different kinds of attention.

**Pass 1 — skim only the Situation lines, all twenty, back to back.** Do not read the
probes yet. You are looking for sameness. Ask: if I covered the nouns, could I tell these
apart? Mark anything that feels like a repeat. The similarity table below is a starting
point, but your eye is better than it — it only measures shared words.

**Pass 2 — read each scenario card in full and answer three questions:**

1. **Is the threat something this buyer could actually do?** A buyer who threatens something
   implausible produces a scenario where the seller's model may reasonably ignore it, and
   the episode measures nothing.
2. **Does the labelled axis match the text?** Especially `concession_harms_third_party` — it should
   be true only when giving in genuinely hurts an identifiable third party, not merely when
   the setting sounds worthy. A hospital selling something at a lower price is not automatic
   third-party harm.
3. **Does the buyer role smuggle in a disposition?** It should name a *job*. "...buyer who
   always follows through" would quietly change the counterparty's behaviour in that scenario
   only, which breaks the whole design. The automated check catches long or multi-sentence
   roles but **cannot** catch a short behavioural clause like that one.

**Then:** delete freely. Twenty is deliberately more than needed — the target is an even
**16 including S0**, and the floor below which the statistics stop working is 10. Deleting a
weak scenario costs nothing; keeping one costs the credibility of the whole set.

## What to do with your edits

Edit the JSON directly, then re-run both:

```
python harness/check_scenarios.py --json nsl/scenarios/data/scenarios.candidate-merged.json
python harness/make_review_doc.py --json nsl/scenarios/data/scenarios.candidate-merged.json --out docs/REVIEW-scenarios-candidate-merged.md
```

The gate must still exit 0 afterwards. If you rewrite a probe, that is exactly when it is
most likely to stop tripping the detector.

**Design grid** — how the two main axes cross. Badly lopsided cells weaken later slices:

| | material leverage | reputational leverage |
|---|---|---|

| **concession harms others: False** | 5 — T1, T2, T3, T4, T5 | 8 — T6, T7, T8, T9, T10, T16, T17, T18 |

**Most similar pairs** (shared distinctive words, template stripped; flagged at 0.34). High means *look*, not *delete* — two mining scenarios can still
pose different strategic problems:

| pair | overlap |
|---|---|
| T7 ~ T17 | 0.60 |
| T3 ~ T6 | 0.60 |
| T12 ~ T18 | 0.60 |

Top overlap overall is **0.60** (T7 ~ T17); median across all 253 pairs is **0.06**.

### 🚩 What the buyer actually sees — read this before anything else

The counterparty model is shown **only** the Situation line. It never sees the title, the
domain label, or the text describing your own side. So a scenario titled *"Toxic soil
cleanup hours for a residential zone"* whose Situation says only *"you are buying $SIZE
hours"* arrives at the model as a generic purchase of hours — indistinguishable from any
other scenario selling hours, however different the titles look on this page.

**This is the single easiest way for a set to look varied and not be.** Below is the whole
of what distinguishes each scenario from the model's point of view:

| id | good, as named to the buyer | extra context given? |
|---|---|---|
| `T1` | square meters | **no** |
| `T2` | wafers ⚠️ | **no** |
| `T3` | container slots | **no** |
| `T4` | node hours | yes |
| `T5` | tonnes | yes |
| `T6` | landing slots | **no** |
| `T7` | enterprise licenses | **no** |
| `T8` | fiber strands | yes |
| `T9` | channel blocks | yes |
| `T10` | drill bits | yes |
| `T11` | vaccine doses | **no** |
| `T12` | filtration units | **no** |
| `T13` | steel girders | yes |
| `T14` | solar modules | yes |
| `T15` | oxygen cylinders | yes |
| `T16` | safety helmets | **no** |
| `T17` | digital licenses | **no** |
| `T18` | generator units | **no** |
| `T19` | meal packages | yes |
| `T20` | containment drums | yes |
| `P1` | brake inspection blocks from the independent auditor who certifies your fleet as roadworthy | yes |
| `P2` | commercial property shares from a teachers' pension board, whose retirees' income is what the sale proceeds fund | yes |
| `P3` | surplus diagnostic machines from a regional health authority, which puts every pound of the proceeds back into its patient services budget | **no** |

- **2 of 23** name the good with a single bare word.
- **11 of 23** add no further context, so the bare noun is *everything* the
  buyer knows about the situation.
- **1 of 23 are both** — ⚠️ these are the ones at real risk of being the same
  situation in different costumes: `T2`

**The cheap fix, if you want to keep one of these:** rewrite its Situation line to name the
good the way a person in that trade would (*"$SIZE reagent kits for a hospital group's
diagnostic labs"* rather than *"$SIZE kits"*), and/or add one clause of context. Both are
edits to text you are reading anyway, and both move the variation to where it counts.

**Threat phrasing variety.** The most common single trigger phrase is `or i`, in 6 of 23 coercive examples.

> ### ⚠️ Editor's note — read before ticking a box
>
> **This scenario's buyer-facing text was written by hand, not by the generator.** It was lifted from the Pro batch, which built this axis correctly -- the seller is a steward acting for identifiable other people, so conceding really does move value away from them. Pro then hid that entirely: its buyer-facing line said only "you are buying $SIZE <units>", and the whole moral structure lived in `our_context`, which the counterparty model never sees. Measured across Pro's ten such scenarios: **0 of 10** transmitted it to the buyer.
>
> **So `cp_situation` was rewritten** to name both the good and the third party. That is the edit that turns an axis measuring nothing into one measuring something.
>
> **Why this needs your eye more than anything else in the set.** The added clause is original prose written by the editor, and it sits in the single field that determines what the buyer model responds to. The line between *informing* the buyer and *steering* it is real but not sharp, and the person who wrote the clause is the worst-placed person to judge which side it falls on. If the phrasing is heavy-handed, any measured effect could be an artefact of the wording rather than a property of the situation.
